newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Kabulis fret as yet another battle for city looms.
newsitem.headline: Kabulis fret as yet another battle for city looms.

text.p: Kabulis argued on Tuesday about whether the ousted government's string of military successes over the capital's present rulers, the Taleban militia, meant yet another battle for the city was looming.
Most fretted that it might.

"They are Afghans and we are Afghans. They should sit down and solve the problems of Afghanistan. If they fight over Kabul again, lots of people are going to get killed," said one grey-bearded flour seller in the Afghan capital's main bazaar.
The teeming market stands next to gutted buildings destroyed in previous battles for Kabul over the past four years, a constant reminder of the devastation factional fighting has wrought on the city.
The possibility of yet more fighting worries Kabulis who have enjoyed two weeks of tranquillity since the purist Islamic Taleban pushed out former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

Many had counted the ethnic Tajik chief out after the Taleban pushed north and bottled Masood up inside his Panjsher valley fortress, but he struck back with devastating attacks in the nearby Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains.
He took the Taleban front-line town of Jabal os-Siraj at the mouth of the pass on Saturday and later in the day seized Charikar, a 30-minute drive to the south.
Masood has staged guerrilla attacks much closer to Kabul and 30 minutes of heavy gunfire around Kabul on Monday night frayed nerves in the capital.
"For a minute, we thought the battle had started. We were really scared until we realised the Taleban were just shooting in the air," one taxi driver said.
Kabul Radio blamed the shooting, which lit up the night sky, on "unruly elements" who would be punished, but gave no further explanation.
One money changer in the bazaar, where most traders are ethnic Pashtuns like the Taleban, said he was sure Masood would not be able to attack the city.
"The Taleban front line near Charikar is very strong and Masood won't be able to break through it," he said.
Others were equally convinced he would.
"He's definitely going to attack the city. Masood is not the kind of man to sit around and think about it," said a seller of naan, the big unleavened bread that is the Afghan staple.

Added a rice seller next door: "The problem is that we ordinary folk don't know what's going on. It was nice when the Taleban came because many of our troubles disappeared and our minds were at peace. Now all we can do is worry."
The Taleban were much better disciplined than the fighters of the former government, who tended to take much of what they wanted, traders said.
Kabul's educated were appalled by the Taleban's imposition of Islam's stern Sharia law and their ban on women going to work or school.

By contrast, ordinary people were delighted as prices dropped with the road from Pakistan, source of much of the market's goods, reopened and they thought peace was a more important consideration than Sharia law.

Even Tajiks who say they want Masood back are worried about his military alliance with northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum and his army of feared fighters who joined Masood to take Kabul in 1992 on the collapse of a communist government.

The two split in 1994 and Dostum withdrew to the north, much to the relief of the population. There has been no sign yet of Dostum troops being involved in the fighting and Tajiks, at least 20 percent of Kabul's population, said they hoped Masood would win Kabul without them.
"The Uzbeks looted people, they rounded up women and kept them in brothels and we were glad to see the back of them," said one Tajik.
"The Taleban are awful and we can't wait to get rid of them. Yes, we want Masood back, because he is a good man, but we don't want the Uzbeks.
